name: Early wristwatch
summary: The small watch on a leather strap that replaced the pocket watch between 1904 and the 1920s. It has a 28 to 35 mm case with wire lugs, a white enamel dial and luminous numerals. The trench version has a wire guard over the glass.

philosophy.core_thesis: Time must be on the wrist, where a pilot, a soldier or a driver can read it with one glance and no free hand.
design_principles: Make the case 28 to 35 mm wide, so that it fits under a cuff and on a thin wrist.
Fix the strap to the case with wire or fixed lugs, so that the strap does not slip.
Print large Arabic numerals on a white enamel dial for a quick read on a moving wrist.
Paint the numerals and hands with luminous paint, so that the dial shows in the dark.
Cover the glass of a field model with a wire guard that turns a blow.
Seal the case with a screw back and a screw bezel, so that sweat and dust stay out.
Fit a small movement, 25 to 29 mm wide and not more than 8 mm thick.
Cut a long, narrow strap of calf leather with a plain pin buckle.
anti_patterns: A pocket watch case with a bow, pushed on a strap
A large dress dial that jams under a cuff
An engraved lid that hides the dial
A thick domed case that catches on cloth
Tiny numerals that blur on a moving wrist
A fabric strap with beads or jewels

silhouette.shape: A small round or square case, 28 to 35 mm wide, with wire or fixed lugs on a leather strap.
silhouette.line: A flat, compact case with short lugs; the glass stands a little above the bezel.
silhouette.fit: The strap wraps the wrist and the watch lies flat under a cuff.
silhouette.proportion: Case thickness to width about 1 to 4; strap width 14 to 18 mm; strap length 180 to 210 mm.
rules: Keep the lugs short so that the case sits on the top of the wrist.
Make the numerals at least 3 mm tall.
Fit the wire guard to the lugs, not to the glass.
Cut the strap in one piece with a pin buckle and two keepers.

fabrics.rule: Use silver or gold for the case, enamel for the dial, calf leather for the strap, and radium paint for the glow.

methods: screw bezel and screw case back
wire lugs soldered to the case
enamel dial fired on a copper base
construction.closures: A pin buckle closes the leather strap; a small crown winds and sets the watch.
construction.details: A wire guard, a screw-down back, luminous numerals and hands, and a strap of calf leather.

surface.pattern: A plain white dial with black numerals; pale green luminous paint on the numerals; a plain polished case.
surface.gloss: Silver case at 60 to 85 GU; enamel at 80 to 100 GU; strap at 10 to 25 GU.
surface.wear: Silver tarnishes to grey; the luminous paint cracks and glows less; the strap darkens and breaks in a few years.

palette.strategy: Use a white dial and black numerals for legibility, a silver or gold case, and a brown strap. The green of the luminous paint is the one tint.

processes: case turning and soldering of lugs
cutting and sewing of leather straps
making.scale: Jewellers made a few at first; in the First World War armies ordered wristwatches by the thousand, and Swiss factories made them.
making.signs: Wire lugs, a screw back, a wire guard and luminous numerals.

pieces.form: Trench watch with wire lugs and a wire guard
Square case with screwed bezel and short lugs
Narrow strap of calf leather with a pin buckle
White enamel dial with luminous Arabic numerals

evidence.title: Santos de Cartier Galbee, designed by Louis Cartier, 1904 (Design Museum)

emotion.target_response: A sense of the new, active body: time close at hand and ready for flight or war.

modifiers.how: Draw the case as a rectangle in platinum or gold with a black enamel ring and a crocodile strap.

modifiers.request: for the field and the cockpit
modifiers.how: Use a black dial with large luminous numerals, a steel case and a leather or canvas strap.
